case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an employer is required to bear more than a 'de minimis' cost to provide a religious accommodation under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and whether the existing 'undue hardship' standard established in Trans World Airlines v. Hardison should be revisited or clarified.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), which requires employers to reasonably accommodate an employee's sincere religious observance or practice unless doing so would impose an 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business'
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Gerald Groff, an Evangelical Christian postal worker who observes Sunday as a day of rest and worship, argues that the United States Postal Service (USPS) failed to provide a reasonable religious accommodation when it required him to deliver packages on Sundays. Groff contends that the prevailing 'de minimis' cost standard derived from Trans World Airlines v. Hardison (1977) sets an improperly low bar for employers seeking to deny religious accommodations, and that 'undue hardship' under Title VII should require a showing of substantial difficulty or expense — consistent with the plain meaning of the statute — rather than merely more than a trivial burden. He further argues that USPS could have accommodated his Sabbath observance without undue hardship by reassigning his Sunday shifts to other willing employees or volunteers.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Louis DeJoy, as Postmaster General representing USPS, argues that accommodating Groff's Sunday Sabbath observance would impose an undue hardship on the postal service's operations, particularly after USPS entered into a package delivery agreement with Amazon that required Sunday deliveries. The government contends that requiring other employees to cover Groff's Sunday shifts caused operational disruptions, coworker resentment, and morale issues, which collectively constitute more than a de minimis burden under the Hardison standard. Respondent further argues that the existing legal framework is well-settled, workable, and should not be disturbed, and that the Third Circuit correctly applied controlling precedent in ruling against Groff.
key_precedents: Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison, 432 U.S. 63 (1977) — established the 'de minimis' cost standard for undue hardship under Title VII
Ansonia Board of Education v. Philbrook, 479 U.S. 60 (1986) — addressed what constitutes a reasonable accommodation under Title VII
EEOC v. Abercrombie & Fitch Stores, Inc., 575 U.S. 768 (2015) — clarified employer obligations regarding religious discrimination and accommodation
United States v. Seeger, 380 U.S. 163 (1965) — addressed the definition of sincere religious belief
Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990) — addressed free exercise of religion under the First Amendment
Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U.S. 398 (1963) — established compelling interest test for religious freedom claims
Tooley v. Martin-Marietta Corp., 648 F.2d 1239 (9th Cir. 1981) — applied Hardison standard in religious accommodation context
Groff v. DeJoy, 35 F.4th 162 (3d Cir. 2022) — the Third Circuit decision under review

John Roberts.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum — from Justice Thomas's originalism to Justice Sotomayor's purposivism to Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualism — reinforces my view that the textual case here is genuinely strong and not merely a product of any single interpretive methodology. Justice Kagan's framing is particularly aligned with my minimalist instincts: rather than wholesale overruling Hardison, we should clarify that 'undue hardship' means substantial difficulty or expense to the employer's actual business operations, remand for application of that standard, and preserve Hardison's separate seniority-system holding intact. Justice Barrett's observation that coworker inconvenience or morale concerns, standing alone, do not constitute hardship on 'the conduct of the employer's business' as the statute expressly requires is a textually precise point I find compelling and worth incorporating into the majority opinion. As the opinion-assigning Justice, I will write narrowly to hold that Hardison's de minimis language was dicta, that 'undue hardship' requires a substantial burden on business operations, and that we remand — avoiding any broader pronouncements about the scope of religious accommodation that could destabilize the broader Title VII framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum reinforces what the text itself compels: 'undue hardship' means something substantially more burdensome than de minimis cost. Justice Gorsuch's reference to his dissent from denial of certiorari in Small v. Memphis Light, Gas & Water is particularly apt — he correctly identified that Hardison 'dramatically revised — really, undid — Title VII's undue hardship test,' which is precisely the kind of judicial legislation that textualism forbids. Justice Barrett's point that the de minimis language was obiter dictum rather than a holding is critical to my stare decisis analysis: we are not overruling a carefully reasoned statutory interpretation but correcting an erroneous gloss that was never properly before the Hardison Court, and thus the reliance interests that normally counsel restraint are substantially diminished. I would go somewhat further than Chief Justice Roberts's preference for a 'narrow ruling' — while I respect his institutionalist concerns, the text admits of only one reading, and we should state clearly that 'undue hardship' requires substantial difficulty or expense, not merely more than trivial inconvenience, leaving no ambiguity for lower courts to exploit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum — from Justice Thomas's originalist analysis to Justice Sotomayor's and Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualism — reinforces what I find most compelling: the statutory text of § 2000e(j) simply cannot be reconciled with the de minimis gloss Hardison's majority inserted without textual foundation. Justice Gorsuch's reference to his Small v. Memphis Light dissent and the ADA's analogous 'undue hardship' definition as requiring 'significant difficulty or expense' is particularly persuasive corroboration that ordinary legal usage of the phrase demands substantially more than trivial inconvenience. The strongest argument for the respondent — that stare decisis counsels deference to Hardison's longstanding interpretation — is substantially weakened by the research-confirmed reality that the de minimis language was dicta, not a holding, meaning lower courts have been applying a standard that never carried full precedential force. I join Chief Justice Roberts's sensible suggestion that we clarify rather than wholesale overrule Hardison, preserving the seniority system holding while correcting the textual misreading that has systematically disadvantaged religious employees for nearly five decades.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I am gratified by the remarkable unanimity among my colleagues, spanning the full ideological spectrum, that Hardison's de minimis gloss cannot be reconciled with the plain statutory text of 'undue hardship.' Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualist approach resonates deeply with me — her emphasis on remanding for lower courts to apply the substantial burden standard to USPS's specific operational circumstances is the most workable path forward, and it avoids the risk of this Court substituting its own factual judgments for those of the lower courts. I write separately to emphasize what Justice Jackson and I both recognize: the statutory text specifies hardship 'on the conduct of the employer's business,' which means coworker resentment, morale concerns, and the mere inconvenience of voluntary shift-swapping are categorically insufficient — they are burdens on employees, not on the business itself, and allowing such considerations to satisfy 'undue hardship' would perpetuate the very discrimination Congress sought to remedy. The strongest argument for Respondent — that overturning Hardison will create administrative uncertainty and open floodgates of accommodation demands — fails because a substantial burden standard still gives employers meaningful protection against genuinely disruptive accommodations, and the decades of inconsistent circuit splits under de minimis demonstrate that the current standard has already produced the very uncertainty that stare decisis is meant to prevent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The conference has reached remarkable unanimity, and I find my colleagues' textual arguments mutually reinforcing rather than redundant. Justice Barrett's point that coworker inconvenience or morale concerns do not constitute hardship on 'the conduct of the employer's business' as the statute expressly requires is particularly sharp — the statutory text itself does the work of limiting what counts as cognizable hardship, and USPS's primary claimed burdens here fall outside that textual boundary. Justice Gorsuch's invocation of the ADA's analogous 'undue hardship' provision, which Congress defined as 'significant difficulty or expense,' provides powerful cross-statutory confirmation that ordinary legal usage of the phrase demands substantially more than a trivial burden, and I would add that when Congress uses the same phrase across statutes addressing similar accommodation obligations, we should read them consistently. My preferred path remains clarification rather than wholesale overruling — preserving Hardison's seniority system holding while correcting the de minimis gloss — because that narrow approach best serves doctrinal stability while faithfully restoring the statutory text Congress enacted.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I am gratified that my colleagues across the ideological spectrum have converged on the same textual conclusion I reached in my Small v. Memphis Light dissent: 'undue hardship' means what it says, and Hardison's de minimis gloss was judicial legislation masquerading as statutory interpretation. Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualist framing is particularly useful — she correctly identifies that the most institutionally sound path is to clarify rather than wholesale overrule Hardison, preserving its seniority-system holding while correcting the de minimis dictum that lower courts have erroneously elevated into binding law. Justice Barrett's point that coworker inconvenience or morale concerns do not constitute hardship on 'the conduct of the employer's business' — the statute's precise language — is textualist analysis at its finest and forecloses USPS's primary defense here. The strongest argument for Respondent would be reliance interests built up around Hardison's de minimis standard, but as I have consistently maintained, stare decisis cannot rescue a precedent that is plainly irreconcilable with enacted text, particularly when that precedent rested on dicta rather than a considered holding on the statutory question.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum — from Justice Thomas's strict textualism to Justice Sotomayor's pragmatic statutory interpretation — reinforces my conviction that the de minimis standard from Hardison cannot be reconciled with the plain text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j). Justice Kagan's point about the ADA's analogous 'undue hardship' provision being defined as 'significant difficulty or expense' is particularly compelling from an institutionalist standpoint: it demonstrates that Congress understood 'undue hardship' to mean something substantially more demanding than de minimis cost, and consistency across statutory frameworks preserves the Court's credibility as a faithful interpreter of legislative text. I am also persuaded by Justice Barrett's careful observation that coworker inconvenience or morale concerns do not constitute hardship on 'the conduct of the employer's business' as the statute expressly requires — this textual limitation is critical and has been systematically ignored under the de minimis regime. Consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's preference for narrow rulings that preserve institutional legitimacy, I would clarify rather than wholesale overrule Hardison, holding that 'undue hardship' requires substantial difficulty or expense while leaving intact Hardison's seniority system holding.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when textualists and purposivists alike converge on the same statutory reading, that convergence reflects the plain meaning's clarity. Justice Kagan's pragmatic framing resonates with me: the word 'undue' carries genuine semantic weight, and a court committed to reading statutes as written cannot simply excise that modifier and replace it with 'de minimis' without textual warrant. Justice Gorsuch's reference to the ADA's analogous 'undue hardship' definition — requiring 'significant difficulty or expense' — is particularly persuasive as confirmatory evidence of ordinary legal usage, since Congress legislates against a background of established legal vocabulary, and 'undue hardship' in that vocabulary has never meant trivial inconvenience. I would add to my colleagues' analysis that the strongest argument for Respondent — stare decisis — is substantially weakened here because, as the research confirms, Hardison's de minimis language was not a holding but dicta, meaning we are not overruling a precedent so much as correcting lower courts' misapplication of language that was never authoritative in the first place; this distinction is critical to my institutional comfort with the result.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I remain firmly with the Petitioner, and I find the convergence of my colleagues' reasoning across very different judicial methodologies — from Justice Thomas's originalism to Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualism to my own progressive pragmatism — powerfully confirms that the de minimis standard cannot survive honest engagement with the statutory text. Justice Kagan's point that reading 'undue' out of 'undue hardship' renders religion a lesser protected category than race and sex under the very same statute is particularly compelling from my perspective: Congress enacted the 1972 amendment precisely to strengthen protections for religious workers, and a standard so low that coworker resentment or morale concerns — burdens on employees, not on 'the conduct of the employer's business' as the statute specifies — can defeat accommodation is flatly inconsistent with that remedial purpose. The strongest argument for Respondent would be institutional stability and reliance interests built around Hardison, but as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, when a Court-created gloss so dramatically departs from enacted text and produces results Congress could not have intended, clarification is not destabilization — it is fidelity. My background as a public defender reinforces that workers of faith, particularly those in hourly and shift-work positions without bargaining power, deserve the genuine statutory protection Congress promised them, not a judicially-created loophole that effectively nullifies it.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of Title VII Section 701(j) plainly requires employers to show 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business,' a standard that by its ordinary meaning demands substantially more than a de minimis cost. The research confirms that the de minimis language in Hardison was dicta rather than a holding — the Court's actual decision rested on seniority system grounds — meaning lower courts have been applying an improperly derived standard that lacks the force of a true precedential holding. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would clarify rather than wholesale overturn Hardison: the Court should hold that 'undue hardship' requires a showing of substantial burden on the employer's actual business operations, while leaving intact Hardison's separate holding regarding seniority systems. This approach respects institutional legitimacy by correcting a textual misreading without unnecessarily destabilizing the broader Title VII framework, and it avoids the constitutional avoidance concerns that would arise if Title VII's religious accommodation provision were rendered effectively toothless compared to its identically structured protections for other characteristics.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must begin with the plain statutory text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), which uses the phrase 'undue hardship' — a term that by any ordinary public meaning in 1972 connoted something substantially more burdensome than a mere 'de minimis' or trivial cost. The Hardison Court's 'de minimis' gloss was not derived from the statutory text but was effectively judicial legislation that gutted Congress's deliberate choice of the word 'undue,' which plainly modifies 'hardship' to require something excessive or disproportionate, not merely more than trifling. When Congress amended Title VII in 1972 to add the religious accommodation provision, it was responding to courts that were insufficiently protecting religious employees, and the legislative record makes clear that Congress intended a meaningful, not nominal, standard of hardship. Stare decisis cannot save Hardison here because, as I have consistently maintained, fidelity to the enacted text must prevail over erroneous precedent, and Hardison's de minimis standard is plainly irreconcilable with the ordinary meaning of 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business.'

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The plain text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), uses the phrase 'undue hardship,' which by any ordinary meaning of those words requires something substantially more burdensome than a mere 'de minimis' cost — the Hardison majority's interpolation of that phrase into the statute was, as even sympathetic commentators have noted, essentially ipse dixit with no firm textual foundation. As a textualist, I cannot countenance a judicial gloss that effectively rewrites a statutory protection Congress enacted to shield religious employees, reducing a meaningful 'undue hardship' standard to a threshold so low that virtually any inconvenience suffices to deny accommodation. The practical consequences of the de minimis standard have been severe and one-sided, systematically disadvantaging religious employees in ways Congress plainly did not intend when it amended Title VII in 1972 to strengthen religious accommodation requirements. While I am generally cautious about disturbing settled precedent, Hardison's core standard was dictum — the case was decided on seniority system grounds — and stare decisis carries diminished force when the prior decision rested on no coherent statutory interpretation methodology, making this an appropriate case to clarify that 'undue hardship' means substantial difficulty or expense to the employer's business operations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The statutory text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), plainly requires employers to demonstrate 'undue hardship' — a substantial burden — before denying a religious accommodation, and the 'de minimis' cost language from Trans World Airlines v. Hardison, 432 U.S. 63 (1977), was dicta that has been widely recognized as inconsistent with the statute's plain meaning and Congress's remedial intent. As Justice Thomas noted in his Abercrombie & Fitch concurrence, Hardison's comment about the 1972 amendment was 'entirely beside the point,' confirming that the de minimis standard lacks binding precedential force as a holding. From a practical standpoint, the de minimis standard has gutted religious accommodation protections for working people of faith — disproportionately harming those in hourly and shift-work positions who lack the bargaining power to negotiate their schedules — while leaving identical statutory protections for other characteristics like race and sex fully intact, a result Congress could not have intended. USPS's claimed hardships here — coworker inconvenience and morale issues from voluntary shift-swapping — fall far short of the genuine, substantial operational burden that the unambiguous statutory text of 'undue hardship' demands.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The plain text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j) requires employers to show 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business,' and as a pragmatic textualist I cannot reconcile that statutory language with the 'de minimis' cost formulation that emerged from Hardison — a standard the research confirms was essentially a single sentence without supporting factors, not argued by the parties, and untethered to the statutory text. The word 'undue' carries real weight; it means something beyond ordinary or trivial inconvenience, and reading it otherwise renders the accommodation requirement largely illusory and treats religion as a lesser protected category than race or sex under the same statute — a result Congress plainly did not intend. Rather than wholesale overruling Hardison, the most workable and textually coherent path is to clarify that 'undue hardship' means substantial difficulty or expense in the context of the employer's overall business operations, consistent with the statute's plain meaning, while remanding for the lower courts to apply that standard to USPS's specific operational circumstances — a middle-ground approach that preserves doctrinal stability while correcting the interpretive error. This reading also aligns with Ansonia Board of Education v. Philbrook's recognition that the accommodation framework must be genuinely meaningful, and avoids the administrative chaos of an unprincipled de minimis threshold that has produced inconsistent results across circuits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j) requires a showing of 'undue hardship' — a phrase that in ordinary usage at the time of the 1972 amendment meant significant difficulty or expense, not merely a de minimis cost. The Hardison Court's 'de minimis' gloss was at best a strained reading of the statutory text and at worst pure judicial legislation that substituted the Court's policy preferences for Congress's enacted words. As I noted in my dissent from denial of certiorari in Small v. Memphis Light, Gas & Water, Hardison 'dramatically revised — really, undid — Title VII's undue hardship test,' and a textualist cannot in good conscience allow that misreading to stand when the statute's plain meaning is clear. The ADA's analogous 'undue hardship' provision, which Congress defined as requiring 'significant difficulty or expense,' confirms that ordinary legal usage of the phrase demands substantially more than a trivial burden, and USPS has not demonstrated that accommodating Groff's Sabbath observance through shift reassignment rises to that level.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The statutory text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), plainly requires employers to accommodate religious practice unless doing so imposes 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business' — language that by any ordinary reading demands a showing of substantial burden, not merely de minimis cost. The 'de minimis' formulation from Trans World Airlines v. Hardison, 432 U.S. 63 (1977), was not a carefully reasoned holding on the meaning of 'undue hardship' but rather dicta that lower courts have erroneously elevated into a binding bright-line rule, as Justice Marshall recognized in dissent. My institutionalist and textualist commitments counsel that when a Court-created gloss so dramatically departs from the statutory text that Congress actually enacted — and produces results Congress could not have intended — clarification is warranted without necessarily overruling Hardison wholesale. A more faithful reading of 'undue hardship' as requiring substantial difficulty or expense better honors the text, aligns religion with the equal statutory footing Congress afforded it alongside race and sex, and preserves the Court's credibility as a faithful interpreter of legislative enactments.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must begin with the statutory text: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j) requires accommodation unless it imposes 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business.' The phrase 'undue hardship' carries a plain and ordinary meaning — substantial difficulty or burden — that is far more demanding than the 'more than de minimis' formulation that emerged from Hardison's majority opinion. Critically, the research confirms that the de minimis language in Hardison was obiter dictum rather than a precise holding interpreting the statutory text, meaning it lacks the full precedential weight that lower courts have accorded it, and it cannot override the statute's actual language as understood at the time of the 1972 amendment. Applying proper textualist methodology, I would hold that 'undue hardship' means what it says — a substantial burden on the employer's business operations — and remand for application of that standard, while noting that coworker inconvenience or morale concerns, standing alone, do not constitute hardship on 'the conduct of the employer's business' as the statute expressly requires.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The plain statutory text of Title VII Section 701(j) requires employers to accommodate religious practices unless doing so imposes an 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business' — language that by any ordinary reading demands a showing of substantial burden, not merely more than a de minimis cost. The 'de minimis' formulation from Trans World Airlines v. Hardison, 432 U.S. 63 (1977), was not a careful parsing of the statutory text but rather dicta that has since been elevated into a controlling standard that effectively guts the accommodation requirement Congress deliberately enacted. From my perspective as a jurist committed to procedural fairness and equal protection, allowing employers to deny religious accommodation based on trivial inconvenience — including coworker resentment, which is a burden on employees rather than on 'the employer's business' as the statute specifies — creates a framework that systematically disadvantages religious minorities and workers of faith in ways Congress expressly sought to prevent. The proper standard requires employers to demonstrate that accommodation would impose a genuinely significant difficulty or expense on the business itself before the undue hardship exception is triggered, consistent with how 'undue hardship' is understood in analogous statutes like the ADA.

John Roberts.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum — from Justice Thomas's originalist analysis to Justice Sotomayor's and Justice Jackson's purposivist and practical concerns — reinforces my own textual conclusion that 'undue hardship' cannot plausibly mean 'de minimis cost.' Justice Kagan's observation that the de minimis standard emerged as dicta from a specific collective bargaining context, not as a carefully reasoned statutory holding, is particularly persuasive and aligns with my preference for narrow, text-grounded rulings that correct clear interpretive errors without unnecessary constitutional adventurism. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward the narrowest possible holding: clarifying that 'undue hardship' requires substantial difficulty or expense in the context of the employer's overall business operations, while explicitly preserving Hardison's core holding regarding seniority systems and collective bargaining agreements — a formulation that should command a broad majority without inviting the Free Exercise Clause questions that a broader ruling might unnecessarily implicate. The strongest argument for the respondent — that overruling or limiting Hardison disrupts decades of settled employer reliance — is answered by the fact that we are correcting dicta, not a carefully reasoned holding, and that the ADA's analogous 'undue hardship' standard has long operated at a higher threshold without producing unworkable results.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when textualists and purposivists alike conclude that Hardison's de minimis gloss cannot be reconciled with the statutory text, that convergence reflects the plain inadequacy of the 1977 majority's reasoning. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies that the Hardison Court was not even interpreting the statutory text directly but rather EEOC guidelines, which compounds the interpretive error. The strongest argument for the respondent would be reliance interests and stare decisis — employers have structured their accommodation practices around the de minimis standard for nearly five decades — but as I have long maintained, stare decisis carries its least force when a prior decision was itself a departure from the statute's original meaning, and no amount of reliance on a judicial misreading can transform that misreading into law. I would go further than Chief Justice Roberts's narrow approach and explicitly overrule Hardison's de minimis formulation rather than merely 'clarify' it, because the text of § 2000e(j) admits of no construction under which 'undue hardship' — a term of art in 1964 labor law connoting substantial burden — can mean anything as trivial as more than de minimis cost.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when textualists like Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch reach the same conclusion as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson through their respective methodologies, that convergence suggests the statutory text is doing real work here. The strongest argument for the respondent — that congressional inaction over nearly five decades ratifies Hardison's standard — fails under my methodology because legislative silence is an unreliable guide to statutory meaning, especially when the silence may reflect political difficulty in overriding a Supreme Court precedent rather than congressional approval of the interpretation. I would clarify, consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's prudent framing, that we need not wholesale overturn Hardison's seniority-system holding but must correct the lower courts' overbroad application of its de minimis dicta to require a showing of substantial burden on the conduct of the employer's business.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I am gratified by the unanimity of my colleagues across ideological lines, and I find Justice Thomas's textualist and originalist grounding particularly reinforcing — even from a very different methodological starting point, he arrives at the same conclusion that 'undue hardship' cannot mean 'de minimis cost' under any defensible reading of the 1964 and 1972 statutory text. The strongest argument for the respondent would be reliance interests and stare decisis — that employers have structured their operations around the de minimis standard for nearly five decades — but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, that concern is substantially diminished when the precedent being preserved was itself dicta rather than a carefully reasoned holding, and when the practical effect has been to render a statutory protection largely illusory for the very workers Congress sought to protect. I write separately to emphasize that the real-world consequences of the de minimis standard have fallen most heavily on hourly workers, shift employees, and members of minority faiths who lack the leverage to negotiate accommodations individually — precisely the vulnerable populations Title VII was designed to shield — and that correcting this interpretive error is not merely a technical exercise in statutory fidelity but a matter of basic fairness and equal access to the workplace. The proper standard requires employers to demonstrate substantial difficulty or expense to the conduct of the business itself, consistent with the statute's plain text and with the meaningful protection Congress intended.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when textualists like Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett reach the same destination as pragmatists like Justice Sotomayor and myself, the statutory text is doing real work. Justice Thomas's point about the ordinary public meaning of 'undue hardship' as a term of art in 1964 labor and employment law is particularly compelling and reinforces my own view that Hardison's de minimis gloss lacks any defensible textual anchor. The strongest argument for the respondent's position would be reliance interests and stare decisis — employers have structured their accommodation practices around the de minimis standard for nearly five decades — but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, we are not overturning a carefully reasoned holding but rather correcting dicta that was improperly elevated into doctrine, which significantly diminishes the stare decisis concern. From my perspective as a former public defender who has seen how procedural shortcuts systematically disadvantage those with the least bargaining power, the practical consequences of maintaining the de minimis standard fall hardest on hourly workers and religious minorities who cannot negotiate accommodations individually, making the case for correction both textually sound and practically urgent.

John Roberts.reasoning: The statutory text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), plainly uses the phrase 'undue hardship,' which by any ordinary meaning connotes a substantially more significant burden than 'de minimis cost.' As the research materials confirm and as Justice Marshall noted in dissent in Hardison itself, the de minimis language appears to have been dicta rather than a carefully reasoned holding tethered to the statutory text, and lower courts have improperly elevated that dicta into a binding bright-line rule that systematically disadvantages religious employees relative to those protected on other Title VII grounds. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings that preserve institutional legitimacy, I would not wholesale overturn Hardison but would instead clarify that 'undue hardship' requires a showing of substantial difficulty or expense in the context of the employer's overall business operations — a reading faithful to the statutory text that avoids the broader constitutional questions lurking under the Free Exercise Clause. This approach respects stare decisis by acknowledging Hardison's core holding regarding seniority systems and collective bargaining agreements while correcting the lower courts' overbroad application of its dicta.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), plainly requires employers to demonstrate 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business' before refusing religious accommodation — and the ordinary public meaning of 'undue hardship' in 1964 unambiguously connotes a substantial burden, not merely a de minimis cost. The Hardison majority's de minimis gloss was not a faithful exercise in statutory interpretation but rather a policy-driven rewriting of the statute's text, and as I have long maintained, stare decisis carries diminished weight when a prior decision was itself a departure from the statute's original meaning rather than a settled constitutional or common law rule. The phrase 'undue hardship' was a term of art in labor and employment law at the time of enactment, consistently understood to require something significantly more burdensome than a trivial or minimal cost, and Congress's subsequent legislative inaction cannot ratify a judicial misreading of a statute's plain text. Furthermore, permitting employers to satisfy 'undue hardship' merely by pointing to coworker inconvenience — rather than actual hardship to the conduct of the business itself — strays even further from the statutory text, which expressly anchors the hardship inquiry to 'the conduct of the employer's business.'

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I cannot ignore that the plain meaning of 'undue hardship' in 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j) connotes a substantially significant burden — 'undue' by ordinary English usage means excessive or disproportionate, not merely more than trivial. The Hardison Court's 'de minimis cost' gloss was not derived from rigorous statutory analysis of the text Congress enacted in 1972, but rather from an EEOC guideline applicable to pre-amendment facts, making it a policy-driven judicial interpolation that effectively rewrote the statute. Justice Marshall's dissent correctly observed that 'simple English usage' does not permit 'undue hardship' to mean 'more than de minimis cost,' and congressional inaction cannot ratify a standard that so plainly contradicts the statutory text. The proper standard requires employers to demonstrate that the accommodation would impose a substantial burden on the conduct of the employer's business — not merely a trivial inconvenience — before denying a religious accommodation under Title VII.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The plain text of Title VII's 'undue hardship' language, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), clearly contemplates a substantial burden on the employer's business — not the de minimis cost standard that Hardison conjured without textual support, without argument from the parties, and without grounding in lower court decisions. As the research confirms, that standard emerged as essentially unreasoned dicta that has for nearly five decades stripped religious workers of the meaningful protection Congress intended, disproportionately harming workers of minority faiths and those in hourly or shift-based employment who lack bargaining power to negotiate accommodations. From a practical standpoint, the de minimis standard has created a near-automatic escape hatch for employers, allowing them to deny accommodation based on trivial inconveniences or coworker grumbling rather than genuine operational hardship — a result that cannot be reconciled with Congress's deliberate choice of the word 'undue,' which by any ordinary reading signals a significant and meaningful threshold. Restoring 'undue hardship' to its natural meaning — requiring employers to demonstrate a substantial burden on the conduct of the business itself — honors the statute's text, protects vulnerable workers whose religious observance puts them at risk of economic coercion, and corrects an egregious interpretive error that stare decisis should not perpetuate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The statutory text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j) plainly requires 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business,' and as a pragmatic textualist I cannot reconcile that language with a de minimis cost threshold — 'undue' hardship by any ordinary reading connotes something substantially more burdensome than a trivial inconvenience. The research confirms what Justice Marshall argued in dissent in Hardison: the de minimis language was dicta arising from a specific collective bargaining context, not a carefully reasoned statutory holding, and lower courts have improperly elevated it into a categorical bright-line rule that drains the accommodation requirement of meaningful force. Workability and statutory coherence both favor clarifying the standard to require that employers demonstrate a substantial burden — something that genuinely imperils the conduct of the business — before denying accommodation, while preserving flexibility for courts to assess hardship contextually rather than imposing a rigid numerical threshold. This approach honors the compromise Congress struck in 1972 when it added the accommodation requirement, avoids the constitutional avoidance concerns lurking at the intersection of Title VII and the Free Exercise Clause, and produces a rule that EEOC and lower courts can administer with reasonable consistency.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), requires employers to accommodate religious practices unless doing so causes 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business' — a phrase that by any ordinary meaning demands something substantially more burdensome than a mere 'de minimis cost.' As a textualist, I cannot accept that Congress, in enacting and then strengthening this provision through the 1972 amendments, intended 'undue hardship' to mean something as trivial as a trifling inconvenience; the word 'undue' itself signals an excessive or disproportionate burden, not a minimal one. The research confirms that Hardison's de minimis standard was not even a direct interpretation of the statutory text but rather of EEOC guidelines, and that Congress in 1972 deliberately chose 'undue hardship' over the weaker 'serious inconvenience' language — a textual choice the Hardison majority effectively nullified. Stare decisis does not compel adherence to a precedent that so plainly departs from the statutory text, particularly where, as Justice Marshall recognized in dissent, the majority's reasoning was itself strained and the lower courts have applied it to render religious accommodation protections largely illusory.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of Title VII Section 701(j) plainly requires employers to demonstrate 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business,' and the ordinary meaning of 'undue hardship' connotes a substantially more significant burden than 'more than a de minimis cost' — a phrase that appears nowhere in the statutory text. As the research confirms, the de minimis language in Hardison was dicta rather than essential to the holding, meaning lower courts have been applying an extra-statutory gloss that dramatically undercuts Congress's 1972 amendments, which were specifically designed to strengthen religious accommodation protections. My institutionalist approach to precedent does not require perpetuating dicta that contradicts statutory text; rather, judicial restraint here means faithfully applying what Congress actually enacted, and I would clarify that 'undue hardship' requires a showing of substantial difficulty or expense to the employer's business operations. This reading also aligns with the practical workability concern that a coherent, text-grounded standard provides clearer guidance to employers and employees alike than an artificially low threshold that has produced inconsistent circuit-level outcomes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must begin and end with the statutory text: Title VII's § 2000e(j) requires an employer to show 'undue hardship on the conduct of the employer's business' — a phrase that, by its ordinary public meaning in 1964, plainly connotes a substantial burden, not merely a de minimis cost. The word 'undue' means excessive or unreasonable, and 'hardship' denotes significant difficulty or suffering; together they establish a meaningful threshold that the Hardison Court's offhand 'more than de minimis' formulation — which appeared without rigorous textual analysis and was not the holding's primary basis — simply cannot satisfy. Stare decisis does not compel adherence to a misreading of statutory text, particularly where, as here, the lower standard was not carefully derived from the enacted language but rather emerged as dictum that has since calcified into doctrine, causing widespread and demonstrable underprotection of religious employees that Congress could not have intended when it enacted the accommodation requirement in 1972. The proper standard requires employers to demonstrate that the accommodation would impose a substantial burden on the conduct of the business itself, consistent with how analogous 'undue hardship' language functions in the ADA and with the ordinary meaning of the statutory text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The plain text of Title VII's 'undue hardship' language, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), demands a substantially more demanding standard than the de minimis cost threshold that Hardison pronounced without adequate textual grounding. As the research materials confirm, Hardison's de minimis formulation was essentially ipse dixit — lacking a coherent ratio decidendi rooted in statutory interpretation — and the weight of scholarly and judicial criticism, including Judge Thapar's concurrence in Small v. Memphis Light, Gas & Water, underscores that the standard has no defensible textual anchor. From a procedural fairness standpoint, the de minimis standard has systematically disadvantaged religious employees, particularly those from minority faiths and working-class backgrounds who lack bargaining power, by allowing employers to deny accommodations with minimal justification — a result that undermines Title VII's core protective purpose. Consistent with my commitment to practical consequences and equal protection, I would hold that 'undue hardship' requires employers to demonstrate a substantial burden on the conduct of their business before denying a religious accommodation, while leaving intact the broader framework of Hardison to the extent it addresses seniority systems.
